pages.text: A $(thing)quine$() is a program that prints its own source code. It needs two parts: a description of itself, and instructions to copy the description and build from it. Von Neumann found the same two parts in any machine that can build itself - years before DNA showed life does it that way. A computer virus, a gene and a $(thing)meme$() (an idea that spreads because it is good at spreading) are the same trick.

Does a replicator's lineage survive? If each copy makes k copies with probability p_k, the chance q that it ever dies out is the smallest root of q = Σp_k q^k. If the mean number of copies is at most 1, it always dies out; above 1 it escapes destruction with probability 1 − q - for two-or-nothing copies at p = 0.6, one time in three.

In the $(item)Nanite Assembler$(), an Undecidable Kernel with a nanite swarm in Autocatalytic Broth becomes four $(item)Quine Replicators$(). Two replicators, catoms and a processor in nanite slurry are another way to a $(item)Von Neumann Probe$().
A machine whose instructions contain a description of itself and an order to copy it. A von Neumann replicator, a virus, a meme.$(br2)Made in $(item)Nanite Assembler$().
Builds copies of itself from whatever it finds. Put one in a Dyson Array.$(br2)Made in $(item)Nanite Assembler$().
